publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Lisinopril - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Lisinopril
Section: Indications & Usage

Lisinopril is an angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor indicated for: Treatment of hypertension in adult patients and pediatric patients 6 years of age and older; Adjunctive therapy in heart failure; Treatment of acute myocardial infarction within 24 hours.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Lisinopril - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Lisinopril
Section: Dosage & Administration

Hypertension: Initial adult dose is 10 mg once daily. Titrate up to 40 mg daily based on blood pressure response. Heart Failure: Initial dose is 5 mg once daily with diuretics. Myocardial Infarction: 5 mg within 24 hours, followed by 5 mg after 24 hours, then 10 mg daily for 6 weeks.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Lisinopril - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Lisinopril
Section: Contraindications

Lisinopril is contraindicated in patients with a history of angioedema related to previous ACE inhibitor treatment, hereditary or idiopathic angioedema, and co-administration with aliskiren in patients with diabetes.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Lisinopril - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Lisinopril
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Angioedema and Anaphylactoid Reactions: Discontinue Lisinopril immediately. Impaired Renal Function: Monitor serum creatinine periodically. Hyperkalemia: Monitor serum potassium periodically. Hypotension: Risk in volume- or salt-depleted patients.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Lisinopril - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Lisinopril
Section: Adverse Reactions

Common adverse reactions (incidence >= 2%) include headache, dizziness, persistent dry cough, fatigue, diarrhea, nausea, and upper respiratory infection.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Lisinopril - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Lisinopril
Section: Drug Interactions

Diuretics: Excessive reduction of blood pressure. Potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone, triamterene) or potassium supplements: Increased risk of hyperkalemia. NSAIDs: Risk of renal impairment and decreased antihypertensive effect. Lithium: Increased serum lithium levels and toxicity.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Lisinopril - Boxed Warning
content:
Drug: Lisinopril
Section: Boxed Warning

WARNING: FETAL TOXICITY. When pregnancy is detected, discontinue Lisinopril as soon as possible. Drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Amlodipine - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Amlodipine
Section: Indications & Usage

Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker indicated for the treatment of hypertension alone or in combination with other antihypertensive agents, and for the management of coronary artery disease (chronic stable angina and vasospastic angina).

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Amlodipine - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Amlodipine
Section: Dosage & Administration

Hypertension: Initial adult dose is 5 mg once daily; maximum dose is 10 mg once daily. Small, fragile, or elderly patients or patients with hepatic insufficiency may be started on 2.5 mg once daily. Chronic Stable or Vasospastic Angina: 5-10 mg daily.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Amlodipine - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Amlodipine
Section: Contraindications

Known hypersensitivity to amlodipine or any of its components.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Amlodipine - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Amlodipine
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Symptomatic hypotension is possible, particularly in patients with severe aortic stenosis. Worsening angina and acute myocardial infarction can develop after starting or increasing the dose, especially in patients with severe obstructive coronary disease. Peripheral edema may occur.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Amlodipine - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Amlodipine
Section: Adverse Reactions

Most common adverse reactions include peripheral edema, dizziness, flushing, palpitations, fatigue, nausea, and somnolence.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Amlodipine - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Amlodipine
Section: Drug Interactions

CYP3A4 Inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, clarithromycin): Increase amlodipine exposure. Simvastatin: Co-administration increases simvastatin exposure (limit simvastatin dose to 20 mg daily with amlodipine). Immunosuppressants (cyclosporine, tacrolimus): Monitor blood levels.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Atorvastatin - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Atorvastatin
Section: Indications & Usage

Atorvastatin is an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor indicated as an adjunct to diet to reduce elevated total cholesterol, LDL-C, apo B, and triglycerides in adults with primary hyperlipidemia, and to reduce the risk of myocardial infarction, stroke, revascularization procedures, and angina in adults with coronary heart disease.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Atorvastatin - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Atorvastatin
Section: Dosage & Administration

Usual starting dose is 10 mg to 20 mg once daily. For patients who require a large reduction in LDL-C (> 45%), starting dose is 40 mg once daily. Dosage range is 10 mg to 80 mg once daily, taken with or without food at any time of day.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Atorvastatin - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Atorvastatin
Section: Contraindications

Active liver disease, including unexplained persistent elevations in hepatic transaminases. Hypersensitivity to any component of this product. Pregnancy and lactation.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Atorvastatin - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Atorvastatin
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Myopathy and Rhabdomyolysis: Rare cases of rhabdomyolysis with acute renal failure secondary to myoglobinuria. Discontinue if markedly elevated CPK levels occur or myopathy is diagnosed. Hepatic Dysfunction: Assess liver enzymes before initiating therapy and as clinically indicated.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Atorvastatin - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Atorvastatin
Section: Adverse Reactions

Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 2%) include nasopharyngitis, arthralgia, diarrhea, pain in extremity, urinary tract infection, and dyspepsia.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Atorvastatin - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Atorvastatin
Section: Drug Interactions

Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, itraconazole, protease inhibitors): Greatly increase atorvastatin exposure and rhabdomyolysis risk; adjust or avoid. Gemfibrozil / Fibrates / Niacin: Increased risk of myopathy. Cyclosporine: Avoid concomitant use or limit dose.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Losartan - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Losartan
Section: Indications & Usage

Losartan potassium is an angiotensin II receptor antagonist indicated for: Treatment of hypertension; Reduction of the risk of stroke in patients with hypertension and left ventricular hypertrophy; Treatment of diabetic nephropathy with an elevated serum creatinine and proteinuria in patients with type 2 diabetes and a history of hypertension.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Losartan - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Losartan
Section: Dosage & Administration

Hypertension: Usual starting dose is 50 mg once daily, with 25 mg used in patients with possible intravascular volume depletion or hepatic impairment. Maximum dose is 100 mg once daily. Diabetic Nephropathy: Starting dose is 50 mg once daily, titrated to 100 mg once daily based on blood pressure response.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Losartan - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Losartan
Section: Contraindications

Hypersensitivity to any component. Do not co-administer aliskiren with Losartan in patients with diabetes.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Losartan - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Losartan
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Fetal toxicity in pregnancy. Hypotension in volume- or salt-depleted patients. Impaired renal function and hyperkalemia.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Losartan - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Losartan
Section: Adverse Reactions

Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 1%) include upper respiratory infection, dizziness, nasal congestion, back pain, and fatigue.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Losartan - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Losartan
Section: Drug Interactions

Potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements: May lead to increases in serum potassium. Lithium: Increases in serum lithium concentrations and lithium toxicity reported. NSAIDs: May lead to increased risk of renal impairment and loss of antihypertensive effect.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Losartan - Boxed Warning
content:
Drug: Losartan
Section: Boxed Warning

WARNING: FETAL TOXICITY. When pregnancy is detected, discontinue Losartan as soon as possible. Drugs that act directly on the renin-angiotensin system can cause injury and death to the developing fetus.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metoprolol Tartrate - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Metoprolol Tartrate
Section: Indications & Usage

Metoprolol tartrate is a selective beta-1-adrenoreceptor blocking agent indicated for the treatment of hypertension, angina pectoris, and hemodynamically stable patients with definite or suspected acute myocardial infarction to reduce cardiovascular mortality.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metoprolol Tartrate - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Metoprolol Tartrate
Section: Dosage & Administration

Hypertension: Initial dose is 100 mg daily in single or divided doses, titrated up to 450 mg daily. Angina Pectoris: Initial dose is 100 mg daily given in two divided doses. Myocardial Infarction: In early phase, 3 bolus injections of 5 mg metoprolol IV followed by 50 mg orally every 6 hours for 48 hours.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metoprolol Tartrate - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Metoprolol Tartrate
Section: Contraindications

Severe bradycardia, second- or third-degree heart block, cardiogenic shock, decompensated heart failure, sick sinus syndrome, and known hypersensitivity.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metoprolol Tartrate - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Metoprolol Tartrate
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Abrupt cessation may precipitate myocardial infarction. Bradycardia and heart block may worsen. Bronchospastic Disease: In general, patients with bronchospastic disease should not receive beta-blockers. Masking of hypoglycemic symptoms in diabetic patients.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metoprolol Tartrate - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Metoprolol Tartrate
Section: Adverse Reactions

Tiredness, dizziness, depression, bradycardia, hypotension, shortness of breath, diarrhea, nausea, and wheezing.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metoprolol Tartrate - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Metoprolol Tartrate
Section: Drug Interactions

Catecholamine-depleting drugs (reserpine): Additive hypotension and bradycardia. CYP2D6 Inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine, diphenhydramine): Increase metoprolol plasma concentration. Calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem): Significant bradycardia and AV conduction depression.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metoprolol Tartrate - Boxed Warning
content:
Drug: Metoprolol Tartrate
Section: Boxed Warning

WARNING: ISCHEMIC HEART DISEASE. Following abrupt cessation of therapy with certain beta-blocking agents, exacerbations of angina pectoris and, in some cases, myocardial infarction have occurred. When discontinuing chronically administered Lopressor, the dosage should be gradually reduced over a period of 1 - 2 weeks.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Hydrochlorothiazide - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Hydrochlorothiazide
Section: Indications & Usage

Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic indicated as adjunctive therapy in edema associated with congestive heart failure, hepatic cirrhosis, and corticosteroid therapy, and in the management of hypertension as a sole agent or to enhance the effectiveness of other antihypertensives.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Hydrochlorothiazide - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Hydrochlorothiazide
Section: Dosage & Administration

Hypertension: Initial dose is 12.5 mg to 25 mg once daily; maximum recommended dose is 50 mg daily. Edema: 25 mg to 100 mg daily in single or divided doses.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Hydrochlorothiazide - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Hydrochlorothiazide
Section: Contraindications

Anuria. Hypersensitivity to hydrochlorothiazide or other sulfonamide-derived drugs.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Hydrochlorothiazide - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Hydrochlorothiazide
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Electrolyte and Metabolic Abnormalities: Hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypochloremic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, and hypercalcemia. Hyperuricemia and precipitation of gout. Acute Myopia and Secondary Angle-Closure Glaucoma. Systemic lupus erythematosus exacerbation.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Hydrochlorothiazide - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Hydrochlorothiazide
Section: Adverse Reactions

Weakness, hypotension including orthostatic hypotension, pancreatitis, jaundice, diarrhea, vomiting, aplastic anemia, leukopenia, purpura, photosensitivity, and muscle spasm.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Hydrochlorothiazide - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Hydrochlorothiazide
Section: Drug Interactions

Antidiabetic drugs: Dosage adjustment of insulin and oral antidiabetic agents may be required. Lithium: Diuretics reduce the renal clearance of lithium and add a high risk of lithium toxicity. NSAIDs: Can reduce diuretic and antihypertensive effects.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metformin - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Metformin
Section: Indications & Usage

Metformin hydrochloride is a biguanide indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients 10 years of age and older with type 2 diabetes mellitus.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metformin - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Metformin
Section: Dosage & Administration

Adult Starting Dose: 500 mg orally twice a day with meals or 850 mg once a day. Titrate by 500 mg weekly or 850 mg every 2 weeks up to a maximum daily dose of 2000 mg to 2550 mg in divided doses. Pediatric (10-16 yrs): 500 mg twice daily up to 2000 mg daily.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metformin - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Metformin
Section: Contraindications

Severe renal impairment (eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73 m²). Known hypersensitivity to metformin. Acute or chronic metabolic acidosis, including diabetic ketoacidosis.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metformin - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Metformin
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Lactic Acidosis risk. Renal Impairment: Assess renal function prior to initiation and periodically thereafter. Iodinated Contrast: Discontinue metformin at the time of or prior to iodinated contrast imaging in patients with eGFR between 30 and 60 mL/min. Vitamin B12 Deficiency: Metformin may lower vitamin B12 levels; monitor hematologic parameters annually.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metformin - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Metformin
Section: Adverse Reactions

Most common adverse reactions (incidence > 5%) are diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, flatulence, abdominal discomfort, indigestion, asthenia, and headache.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metformin - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Metformin
Section: Drug Interactions

Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (topiramate, zonisamide): Increase risk of lactic acidosis. Cationic drugs eliminated by renal tubular secretion (cimetidine, ranolazine, dolutegravir): May increase metformin plasma concentrations. Alcohol: Potentiates metformin effect on lactate metabolism.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Metformin - Boxed Warning
content:
Drug: Metformin
Section: Boxed Warning

WARNING: LACTIC ACIDOSIS. Post-marketing cases of metformin-associated lactic acidosis have resulted in death, hypothermia, hypotension, and resistant bradyarrhythmias. Risk factors include renal impairment, concomitant use of certain drugs (e.g., carbonic anhydrase inhibitors), age 65 or greater, radiological studies with iodinated contrast, surgery, hypoxic states, and excessive alcohol intake. If lactic acidosis is suspected, immediately discontinue Metformin and institute prompt hemodialysis.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Glipizide - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Glipizide
Section: Indications & Usage

Glipizide is a second-generation sulfonylurea indicated as an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Glipizide - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Glipizide
Section: Dosage & Administration

Immediate-Release: Starting dose is 5 mg daily given before breakfast. Titrate in increments of 2.5 to 5 mg up to a maximum recommended single dose of 15 mg or total daily dose of 40 mg. Extended-Release (XL): Starting dose is 5 mg once daily with breakfast, maximum 20 mg daily.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Glipizide - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Glipizide
Section: Contraindications

Known hypersensitivity to glipizide or sulfonamides. Type 1 diabetes mellitus and diabetic ketoacidosis.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Glipizide - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Glipizide
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Hypoglycemia: All sulfonylurea drugs are capable of producing severe hypoglycemia; elderly, debilitated, or malnourished patients and those with adrenal or renal insufficiency are particularly susceptible. Hemolytic Anemia: In patients with G6PD deficiency, sulfonylureas can cause hemolytic anemia. Increased risk of cardiovascular mortality based on UGDP study.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Glipizide - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Glipizide
Section: Adverse Reactions

Hypoglycemia, dizziness, diarrhea, nervousness, flatulence, tremor, skin rash, pruritus, and urticaria.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Glipizide - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Glipizide
Section: Drug Interactions

Certain drugs tend to produce hypoglycemia and potentiate glipizide action: NSAIDs, salicylates, sulfonamides, chloramphenicol, probenecid, coumarins, MAOIs, and beta-blockers. Drugs that produce hyperglycemia and decrease control: Thiazide diuretics, corticosteroids, phenothiazines, thyroid hormones, estrogens, and oral contraceptives.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Empagliflozin - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Empagliflozin
Section: Indications & Usage

Empagliflozin is an SGLT2 inhibitor indicated: As an adjunct to diet and exercise to improve glycemic control in adults and pediatric patients aged 10 years and older with type 2 diabetes; To reduce the risk of cardiovascular death in adults with type 2 diabetes and established cardiovascular disease; To reduce the risk of cardiovascular death and hospitalization for heart failure in adults with heart failure; To reduce the risk of sustained eGFR decline in adults with chronic kidney disease.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Empagliflozin - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Empagliflozin
Section: Dosage & Administration

The recommended dose of empagliflozin is 10 mg once daily in the morning, taken with or without food. In patients tolerating 10 mg daily who require additional glycemic control, the dose may be increased to 25 mg once daily. Assess renal function before initiation.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Empagliflozin - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Empagliflozin
Section: Contraindications

Severe hypersensitivity reaction to empagliflozin or any excipients. Patients on dialysis.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Empagliflozin - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Empagliflozin
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Ketoacidosis: Serious, life-threatening cases of ketoacidosis in type 1 and type 2 diabetes regardless of blood glucose levels (euglycemic ketoacidosis). Volume Depletion: Symptomatic hypotension can occur, particularly in patients with renal impairment, elderly patients, or patients on loop diuretics. Urosepsis and Pyelonephritis: Serious urinary tract infections. Necrotizing Fasciitis of the Perineum (Fournier's Gangrene): Rare life-threatening bacterial infection. Lower Limb Amputation risk.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Empagliflozin - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Empagliflozin
Section: Adverse Reactions

Urinary tract infections, female genital mycotic infections, upper respiratory tract infections, increased urination, dyslipidemia, arthralgia, and thirst.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Empagliflozin - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Empagliflozin
Section: Drug Interactions

Co-administration with insulin or insulin secretagogues increases the risk of hypoglycemia; a lower dose of insulin or secretagogue may be required. Co-administration with diuretics causes additive volume depletion and hypotension.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Amoxicillin - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Amoxicillin
Section: Indications & Usage

Amoxicillin is a penicillin-class antibacterial indicated for the treatment of infections due to susceptible isolates of designated microorganisms in: Infections of the ear, nose, and throat (Streptococcus spp., S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae); Infections of the genitourinary tract (E. coli, P. mirabilis, E. faecalis); Infections of the skin and skin structure; Lower respiratory tract infections; Triple therapy for Helicobacter pylori eradication.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Amoxicillin - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Amoxicillin
Section: Dosage & Administration

Adults: 500 mg every 12 hours or 250 mg every 8 hours for mild-to-moderate infections. For severe infections, 875 mg every 12 hours or 500 mg every 8 hours. Pediatric Patients (> 3 months): 20 to 45 mg/kg/day in divided doses every 8 or 12 hours.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Amoxicillin - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Amoxicillin
Section: Contraindications

Known serious hypersensitivity reaction (e.g., anaphylaxis or Stevens-Johnson syndrome) to amoxicillin or other beta-lactam antibacterial drugs (e.g., penicillins and cephalosporins).

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Amoxicillin - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Amoxicillin
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Serious and occasionally fatal hypersensitivity (anaphylactic) reactions have been reported in patients on penicillin therapy. Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) ranging from mild diarrhea to fatal colitis. Development of drug-resistant bacteria if prescribed without proven bacterial infection. Rash in patients with mononucleosis.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Amoxicillin - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Amoxicillin
Section: Adverse Reactions

Most common adverse reactions (> 1%) are diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, skin rashes, urticaria, and vaginitis.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Amoxicillin - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Amoxicillin
Section: Drug Interactions

Probenecid: Decreases renal tubular secretion of amoxicillin, producing higher and prolonged blood levels. Oral Anticoagulants (warfarin): May prolong prothrombin time; monitor INR closely. Allopurinol: Concomitant administration substantially increases the incidence of skin rashes. Oral Contraceptives: May decrease contraceptive efficacy.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Azithromycin - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Azithromycin
Section: Indications & Usage

Azithromycin is a macrolide antibacterial indicated for mild to moderate infections caused by designated susceptible bacteria in: Acute bacterial exacerbations of chronic bronchitis; Acute bacterial sinusitis; Community-acquired pneumonia; Pharyngitis/tonsillitis; Uncomplicated skin and skin structure infections; Urethritis and cervicitis due to Chlamydia trachomatis; Genital ulcer disease in men due to Haemophilus ducreyi.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Azithromycin - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Azithromycin
Section: Dosage & Administration

Community-Acquired Pneumonia / Skin Infections: 500 mg as a single dose on Day 1, followed by 250 mg once daily on Days 2 through 5 (Z-Pak regimen). Acute Sinusitis: 500 mg once daily for 3 days. Genital Chlamydial Infection: Single 1 gram (1000 mg) dose.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Azithromycin - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Azithromycin
Section: Contraindications

Hypersensitivity to azithromycin, erythromycin, or any macrolide or ketolide. History of cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction associated with prior use of azithromycin.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Azithromycin - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Azithromycin
Section: Warnings & Precautions

QT Interval Prolongation: Can cause prolonged cardiac repolarization and QT interval, imparting risk of cardiac arrhythmia and torsades de pointes. Fatalities reported in elderly patients and those with preexisting cardiac risk factors. Hepatotoxicity: Abnormal liver function, hepatitis, cholestatic jaundice, hepatic necrosis, and hepatic failure reported. Infantile Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (IHPS). Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD).

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Azithromycin - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Azithromycin
Section: Adverse Reactions

Diarrhea/loose stools, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, headache, dizziness, and vaginitis.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Azithromycin - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Azithromycin
Section: Drug Interactions

Nelfinavir: Increases azithromycin serum concentrations. Warfarin: Monitor prothrombin time/INR. Digoxin, Colchicine: Concomitant administration with macrolides can elevate serum levels of P-gp substrates. Drugs prolonging QT interval (amiodarone, quinidine, sotalol): Increased risk of fatal arrhythmias.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Ciprofloxacin - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Ciprofloxacin
Section: Indications & Usage

Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibacterial indicated in adults for the treatment of urinary tract infections, chronic bacterial prostatitis, lower respiratory tract infections, acute sinusitis, skin and skin structure infections, bone and joint infections, complicated intra-abdominal infections, infectious diarrhea, and post-exposure inhalational anthrax.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Ciprofloxacin - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Ciprofloxacin
Section: Dosage & Administration

Urinary Tract Infections: 250 mg to 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 to 14 days. Lower Respiratory / Skin / Bone: 500 mg to 750 mg orally every 12 hours for 7 to 14 days (up to 4-6 weeks for bone infections). Post-exposure Anthrax: 500 mg orally every 12 hours for 60 days.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Ciprofloxacin - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Ciprofloxacin
Section: Contraindications

Known hypersensitivity to ciprofloxacin or any other quinolones. Concomitant administration with tizanidine (causes severe hypotension and sedation due to CYP1A2 inhibition).

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Ciprofloxacin - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Ciprofloxacin
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Disabling and potentially irreversible serious adverse reactions (tendon rupture, neuropathy, CNS toxicities including seizures, psychosis, and toxic psychosis). Aortic aneurysm and dissection: Increased risk within 2 months of use. Blood glucose disturbances: Hypoglycemia coma reported in elderly diabetics. QT prolongation.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Ciprofloxacin - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Ciprofloxacin
Section: Adverse Reactions

Nausea, diarrhea, liver function test abnormalities, vomiting, rash, headache, restlessness, insomnia, and abdominal pain.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Ciprofloxacin - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Ciprofloxacin
Section: Drug Interactions

Tizanidine: Contraindicated (CYP1A2 inhibition). Theophylline: Significant increase in theophylline toxicity; monitor blood levels. Multivalent Cation-Containing Products (antacids with magnesium/aluminum, iron supplements, calcium, dairy): Markedly reduce ciprofloxacin absorption; administer ciprofloxacin at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Ciprofloxacin - Boxed Warning
content:
Drug: Ciprofloxacin
Section: Boxed Warning

WARNING: SERIOUS ADVERSE REACTIONS INCLUDING TENDINITIS, TENDON RUPTURE, PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY, CENTRAL NERVOUS SYSTEM EFFECTS AND EXACERBATION OF MYASTHENIA GRAVIS. Fluoroquinolones, including Ciprofloxacin, have been associated with disabling and potentially irreversible serious adverse reactions that have occurred together including tendinitis and tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and CNS effects. Discontinue Ciprofloxacin immediately if a patient experiences any of these serious adverse reactions. In patients with myasthenia gravis, fluoroquinolones may exacerbate muscle weakness. Avoid ciprofloxacin in patients with known history of myasthenia gravis.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Doxycycline - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Doxycycline
Section: Indications & Usage

Doxycycline is a tetracycline-class antibacterial indicated for rickettsial infections (Rocky Mountain spotted fever, typhus), sexually transmitted infections (chlamydia, lymphogranuloma venereum), respiratory tract infections (Mycoplasma pneumoniae), anthrax (inhalational), Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi), malaria prophylaxis (Plasmodium falciparum), and severe acne vulgaris.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Doxycycline - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Doxycycline
Section: Dosage & Administration

Adults: Usual dose is 200 mg on the first day of treatment (100 mg every 12 hours) followed by a maintenance dose of 100 mg once daily or 50 mg every 12 hours. Severe infections: 100 mg every 12 hours. Administration with adequate amounts of fluid is recommended to wash down the drug and reduce risk of esophageal irritation and ulceration.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Doxycycline - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Doxycycline
Section: Contraindications

Hypersensitivity to any of the tetracyclines.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Doxycycline - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Doxycycline
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Tooth Discoloration and Enamel Hypoplasia: Use during tooth development (last half of pregnancy, infancy, and childhood to the age of 8 years) may cause permanent discoloration of teeth (yellow-gray-brown). Inhibition of Bone Growth in premature infants. Photosensitivity manifesting as exaggerated sunburn reaction. Pseudotumor Cerebri (benign intracranial hypertension). Esophageal ulcerations.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Doxycycline - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Doxycycline
Section: Adverse Reactions

Anorexia, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, glossitis, dysphagia, enterocolitis, maculopapular and erythematous rashes, skin hyperpigmentation, and elevated BUN.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Doxycycline - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Doxycycline
Section: Drug Interactions

Anticoagulants: Tetracyclines depress plasma prothrombin activity; decrease anticoagulant dosage. Antacids containing aluminum, calcium, or magnesium and iron preparations: Impair doxycycline absorption. Barbiturates, carbamazepine, and phenytoin: Decrease half-life of doxycycline.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Levothyroxine - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Levothyroxine
Section: Indications & Usage

Synthroid (levothyroxine sodium) is indicated for: Replacement therapy in primary (thyroidal), secondary (pituitary), and tertiary (hypothalamic) congenital or acquired hypothyroidism; Pituitary Thyrotropin (TSH) Suppression as an adjunct to surgery and radioiodine therapy in the management of thyrotropin-dependent well-differentiated thyroid cancer.

metadata.strength: 25 mcg, 50 mcg, 75 mcg, 88 mcg, 100 mcg, 112 mcg, 125 mcg, 137 mcg, 150 mcg, 175 mcg, 200 mcg, 300 mcg

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Levothyroxine - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Levothyroxine
Section: Dosage & Administration

Administer once daily as a single dose, on an empty stomach, one-half to one hour before breakfast with a full glass of water. Full replacement dose in adult patients with primary hypothyroidism without cardiac disease is approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day. In elderly patients or patients with underlying cardiovascular disease, start at 12.5 to 25 mcg/day and titrate every 6-8 weeks based on serum TSH.

metadata.strength: 25 mcg, 50 mcg, 75 mcg, 88 mcg, 100 mcg, 112 mcg, 125 mcg, 137 mcg, 150 mcg, 175 mcg, 200 mcg, 300 mcg

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Levothyroxine - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Levothyroxine
Section: Contraindications

Uncorrected adrenal insufficiency (thyroid hormone increases metabolic clearance of glucocorticoids and may precipitate an acute adrenal crisis). Hypersensitivity to synthetic levothyroxine.

metadata.strength: 25 mcg, 50 mcg, 75 mcg, 88 mcg, 100 mcg, 112 mcg, 125 mcg, 137 mcg, 150 mcg, 175 mcg, 200 mcg, 300 mcg

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Levothyroxine - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Levothyroxine
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Cardiac Adverse Reactions in the Elderly and in Patients with Underlying Cardiovascular Disease (angina, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction). Myxedema Coma requires IV levothyroxine, not oral. Acute Adrenal Crisis in patients with concomitant adrenal insufficiency. Worsening Diabetic Control: May increase insulin or antidiabetic agent requirements. Decreased bone mineral density with overtreatment.

metadata.strength: 25 mcg, 50 mcg, 75 mcg, 88 mcg, 100 mcg, 112 mcg, 125 mcg, 137 mcg, 150 mcg, 175 mcg, 200 mcg, 300 mcg

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Levothyroxine - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Levothyroxine
Section: Adverse Reactions

Adverse reactions of Synthroid are primarily those of hyperthyroidism due to therapeutic overdosage: arrhythmias, tachycardia, palpitation, myocardial infarction, dyspnea, muscle spasms, headache, nervousness, irritability, insomnia, tremors, muscle weakness, increased appetite, weight loss, diarrhea, heat intolerance, and menstrual irregularities.

metadata.strength: 25 mcg, 50 mcg, 75 mcg, 88 mcg, 100 mcg, 112 mcg, 125 mcg, 137 mcg, 150 mcg, 175 mcg, 200 mcg, 300 mcg

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Levothyroxine - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Levothyroxine
Section: Drug Interactions

Calcium carbonate, ferrous sulfate, bile acid sequestrants (cholestyramine, colestipol), sucralfate, aluminum antacids, and proton pump inhibitors: Bind levothyroxine and markedly reduce absorption; separate administration by at least 4 hours. Warfarin: Levothyroxine increases catabolism of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors, potentiating anticoagulant effect. Digoxin: Thyroid hormone increases renal clearance of digoxin.

metadata.strength: 25 mcg, 50 mcg, 75 mcg, 88 mcg, 100 mcg, 112 mcg, 125 mcg, 137 mcg, 150 mcg, 175 mcg, 200 mcg, 300 mcg

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Levothyroxine - Boxed Warning
content:
Drug: Levothyroxine
Section: Boxed Warning

WARNING: NOT FOR TREATMENT OF OBESITY OR FOR WEIGHT LOSS. Thyroid hormones, including Synthroid, either alone or with other therapeutic agents, should not be used for the treatment of obesity or for weight loss. In euthyroid patients, doses within the range of daily hormonal requirements are ineffective for weight reduction. Larger doses may produce serious or even life-threatening manifestations of toxicity, particularly when given in association with sympathomimetic amines such as those used for their anorectic effects.

metadata.strength: 25 mcg, 50 mcg, 75 mcg, 88 mcg, 100 mcg, 112 mcg, 125 mcg, 137 mcg, 150 mcg, 175 mcg, 200 mcg, 300 mcg

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Prednisone - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Prednisone
Section: Indications & Usage

Prednisone is a synthetic glucocorticoid indicated for: Endocrine disorders (adrenal insufficiency); Rheumatic disorders (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis); Collagen diseases (systemic lupus erythematosus, acute rheumatic carditis); Dermatologic diseases (pemphigus, severe erythema multiforme); Allergic states (severe asthma, contact dermatitis); Ophthalmic diseases; Respiratory diseases; Hematologic disorders (autoimmune hemolytic anemia); Neoplastic diseases (leukemias and lymphomas); Edematous states (nephrotic syndrome); Acute exacerbations of multiple sclerosis.

metadata.strength: 1 mg, 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, 50 mg

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Prednisone - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Prednisone
Section: Dosage & Administration

Initial dosage may vary from 5 mg to 60 mg per day depending on the specific disease entity being treated. In situations of less severity, lower doses will generally suffice, while in selected patients higher initial doses may be required. When discontinuing prolonged therapy, the dosage must be tapered gradually rather than stopped abruptly to prevent secondary adrenocortical insufficiency.

metadata.strength: 1 mg, 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, 50 mg

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Prednisone - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Prednisone
Section: Contraindications

Systemic fungal infections. Known hypersensitivity to prednisone or its components.

metadata.strength: 1 mg, 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, 50 mg

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Prednisone - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Prednisone
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Hypothalamic-Pituitary-Adrenal (HPA) Axis Suppression and Acute Adrenal Crisis upon abrupt withdrawal. Immunosuppression and Increased Risk of Infections: Glucocorticoids mask signs of infection and new infections may appear during use; chickenpox and measles can have serious/fatal course in non-immune patients. Peptic Ulceration and Gastrointestinal Perforation. Ophthalmic Effects: Cataracts, glaucoma, and ocular infections. Osteoporosis and Aseptic Necrosis of bone. Psychiatric Disturbances (euphoria, insomnia, mood swings, psychosis). Hyperglycemia and worsening diabetes. Fluid retention and hypertension.

metadata.strength: 1 mg, 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, 50 mg

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Prednisone - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Prednisone
Section: Adverse Reactions

Fluid retention, sodium retention, potassium loss, hypokalemic alkalosis, muscle weakness, osteoporosis, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, cushingoid state, growth suppression in children, impaired wound healing, thin fragile skin, petechiae, facial erythema, convulsions, vertigo, headache, and menstrual irregularities.

metadata.strength: 1 mg, 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, 50 mg

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Prednisone - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Prednisone
Section: Drug Interactions

NSAIDs (aspirin, ibuprofen): Concomitant use increases risk of gastrointestinal ulceration and bleeding. Antidiabetic agents: Glucocorticoids raise blood glucose; antidiabetic dose increase required. Phenytoin, Phenobarbital, Rifampin: CYP3A4 inducers increase hepatic metabolism of prednisone and decrease efficacy. Live Vaccines: Live virus vaccines are contraindicated in patients receiving immunosuppressive doses of corticosteroids.

metadata.strength: 1 mg, 2.5 mg, 5 mg, 10 mg, 20 mg, 50 mg

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Gabapentin - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Gabapentin
Section: Indications & Usage

Gabapentin is indicated for: Management of postherpetic neuralgia in adults; Adjunctive therapy in the treatment of partial onset seizures, with and without secondary generalization, in adults and pediatric patients 3 years of age and older with epilepsy.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Gabapentin - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Gabapentin
Section: Dosage & Administration

Postherpetic Neuralgia: Day 1: 300 mg once daily; Day 2: 300 mg twice daily; Day 3: 300 mg three times daily. Titrate up to 1800 mg/day (600 mg three times daily). Epilepsy (Adults): Starting dose is 300 mg three times daily. Maintenance dose is 900 to 1800 mg/day in three divided doses; maximum dose is 2400 to 3600 mg/day. Dose must be adjusted in patients with reduced renal function (CrCl < 60 mL/min).

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Gabapentin - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Gabapentin
Section: Contraindications

Known hypersensitivity to gabapentin or its ingredients.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Gabapentin - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Gabapentin
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Antiepileptic Drugs (AEDs) and Suicidal Behavior: Increases the risk of suicidal thoughts or behavior. Monitor for depression or unusual mood changes. Respiratory Depression: Serious, life-threatening hypoventilation when co-administered with central nervous system (CNS) depressants (opioids) or in patients with underlying respiratory impairment. Somnolence and Dizziness: Impairs ability to drive or operate machinery. Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms (DRESS / Multiorgan Hypersensitivity). Abrupt discontinuation may increase seizure frequency.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Gabapentin - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Gabapentin
Section: Adverse Reactions

Most common adverse reactions in postherpetic neuralgia: dizziness, somnolence, peripheral edema, infection, ataxia, and blurred vision. In epilepsy: somnolence, dizziness, ataxia, fatigue, and nystagmus.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Gabapentin - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Gabapentin
Section: Drug Interactions

Opioids (morphine, oxycodone): Co-administration increases gabapentin concentrations and markedly increases risk of CNS depression and fatal respiratory depression. Antacids (Maalox): Reduce gabapentin bioavailability by about 20%; take gabapentin at least 2 hours after antacid.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Levetiracetam - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Levetiracetam
Section: Indications & Usage

Levetiracetam is an antiepileptic drug indicated for: Adjunctive therapy in the treatment of partial-onset seizures in patients 1 month of age and older; Adjunctive therapy in the treatment of myoclonic seizures in patients 12 years of age and older with juvenile myoclonic epilepsy; Adjunctive therapy in the treatment of primary generalized tonic-clonic seizures in patients 6 years of age and older with idiopathic generalized epilepsy.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Levetiracetam - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Levetiracetam
Section: Dosage & Administration

Adults (16 years and older): Initiate treatment with a daily dose of 1000 mg/day, given as 500 mg twice daily. Increase dose by 1000 mg/day every 2 weeks up to a maximum recommended daily dose of 3000 mg/day (1500 mg twice daily). Renal impairment: Adjust dose based on creatinine clearance (e.g., CrCl 50-80 mL/min: 500-1000 mg q12h; CrCl < 30 mL/min: 250-500 mg q12h).

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Levetiracetam - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Levetiracetam
Section: Contraindications

Known hypersensitivity to levetiracetam; angioedema and anaphylaxis have occurred.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Levetiracetam - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Levetiracetam
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Behavioral Abnormalities and Psychotic Symptoms: May cause somnolence, fatigue, irritability, aggression, agitation, anger, depression, and psychosis. Suicidal Behavior and Ideation: Monitor for emergence of suicidal thoughts. Serious Dermatologic Reactions: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN). Anaphylaxis and Angioedema. Withdrawal Seizures: As with all AEDs, withdraw gradually.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Levetiracetam - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Levetiracetam
Section: Adverse Reactions

Somnolence, asthenia, infection, dizziness, nasopharyngitis, fatigue, decreased appetite, irritability, and headache.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Levetiracetam - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Levetiracetam
Section: Drug Interactions

Levetiracetam does not inhibit or induce hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes. No significant pharmacokinetic interactions observed with other antiepileptic drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate, lamotrigine, gabapentin, phenobarbital). Probenecid: Inhibits renal tubular clearance of levetiracetam metabolite.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Albuterol - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Albuterol
Section: Indications & Usage

Albuterol sulfate inhalation aerosol is a beta-2-adrenergic agonist indicated for: Treatment or prevention of bronchospasm in adult and pediatric patients aged 4 years and older with reversible obstructive airway disease (asthma, COPD); Prevention of exercise-induced bronchospasm (EIB) in patients aged 4 years and older.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Albuterol - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Albuterol
Section: Dosage & Administration

Acute Bronchospasm: 2 inhalations (180 mcg) every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Prevention of Exercise-Induced Bronchospasm: 2 inhalations 15 to 30 minutes before exercise. Prime the inhaler before first use and when inhaler has not been used for > 2 weeks.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Albuterol - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Albuterol
Section: Contraindications

Hypersensitivity to albuterol or any of the ingredients.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Albuterol - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Albuterol
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Paradoxical Bronchospasm: Life-threatening paradoxical bronchospasm may occur with acute wheezing; discontinue immediately and treat with alternative therapy. Cardiovascular Effects: Produces clinically significant cardiovascular effects in some patients as measured by pulse rate, blood pressure, and ECG changes (tachycardia, palpitations, arrhythmias). Immediate Hypersensitivity Reactions. Hypokalemia and Hyperglycemia. Excessive use can be fatal.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Albuterol - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Albuterol
Section: Adverse Reactions

Tremor, nervousness, headache, dizziness, insomnia, tachycardia, palpitations, nausea, vomiting, throat irritation, upper respiratory tract infection, and cough.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Albuterol - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Albuterol
Section: Drug Interactions

Beta-Blockers (propranolol): Inhibit the bronchodilator effect of albuterol and may produce severe bronchospasm in patients with asthma. Diuretics: Non-potassium-sparing diuretics (loop or thiazides) can worsen ECG changes and hypokalemia. Digoxin: May decrease serum digoxin levels. Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (MAOIs) and Tricyclic Antidepressants (TCAs): Potentiate action of albuterol on cardiovascular system.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Fluticasone Propionate - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Fluticasone Propionate
Section: Indications & Usage

Flovent HFA is an inhaled corticosteroid indicated for maintenance treatment of asthma as prophylactic therapy in adult and pediatric patients aged 4 years and older. Important limitation: Not indicated for relief of acute bronchospasm.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Fluticasone Propionate - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Fluticasone Propionate
Section: Dosage & Administration

Administer by oral inhalation twice daily (morning and evening). Adult starting dose depends on asthma severity: Patients previously on bronchodilators alone: 88 mcg twice daily (maximum 440 mcg twice daily); Patients previously on inhaled corticosteroids: 88 to 220 mcg twice daily (maximum 880 mcg twice daily). Rinse mouth with water without swallowing after inhalation to reduce risk of oropharyngeal candidiasis.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Fluticasone Propionate - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Fluticasone Propionate
Section: Contraindications

Primary treatment of status asthmaticus or other acute episodes of asthma where intensive measures are required. Known severe hypersensitivity to fluticasone propionate.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Fluticasone Propionate - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Fluticasone Propionate
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Oropharyngeal Candidiasis (thrush): Fungal infection of mouth and pharynx occurs in some patients; rinse mouth with water after inhalation. Immunosuppression and Increased Risk of Infections (chickenpox, measles, tuberculosis). Transferring Patients from Systemic Corticosteroid Therapy: Risk of adrenal insufficiency. Hypercorticism and Adrenal Suppression with high doses. Reduction in Bone Mineral Density. Growth Effects in Children: Monitor growth of pediatric patients. Glaucoma and Cataracts.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Fluticasone Propionate - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Fluticasone Propionate
Section: Adverse Reactions

Upper respiratory tract infection, throat irritation, sinusitis, candidiasis (oral thrush), cough, bronchitis, headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and dysphonia (hoarseness).

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Fluticasone Propionate - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Fluticasone Propionate
Section: Drug Interactions

Strong Cytochrome P450 3A4 Inhibitors (ritonavir, ketoconazole, clarithromycin, itraconazole): Concomitant use increases plasma fluticasone propionate exposure, leading to systemic corticosteroid effects, Cushing's syndrome, and adrenal suppression. Avoid co-administration with ritonavir.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Omeprazole - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Omeprazole
Section: Indications & Usage

Omeprazole is a proton pump inhibitor indicated for: Treatment of active duodenal ulcer; Treatment of active benign gastric ulcer; Treatment of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD); Maintenance of healing of erosive esophagitis; Pathological hypersecretory conditions (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome); Eradication of Helicobacter pylori in combination with clarithromycin and amoxicillin.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Omeprazole - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Omeprazole
Section: Dosage & Administration

Take before eating, preferably in the morning. Swallow capsules whole; do not chew or crush. Active Duodenal Ulcer: 20 mg once daily for 4 weeks. Gastric Ulcer: 40 mg once daily for 4 to 8 weeks. GERD / Erosive Esophagitis: 20 mg once daily for 4 to 8 weeks. Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome: Starting dose is 60 mg once daily, adjusted up to 120 mg three times daily.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Omeprazole - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Omeprazole
Section: Contraindications

Known hypersensitivity to omeprazole or other substituted benzimidazoles (e.g., esomeprazole, lansoprazole, pantoprazole). Co-administration with rilpivirine-containing products.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Omeprazole - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Omeprazole
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Gastric Malignancy: Symptomatic response to therapy does not preclude presence of gastric malignancy. Acute Tubulointerstitial Nephritis. Clostridioides difficile-Associated Diarrhea (CDAD). Bone Fracture: Long-term and multiple daily dose therapy associated with increased risk of osteoporosis-related fractures of hip, wrist, or spine. Cutaneous and Systemic Lupus Erythematosus. Vitamin B12 (Cyanocobalamin) Deficiency with daily long-term use (> 3 years). Hypomagnesemia with prolonged use (> 1 year). Fundic gland polyps.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Omeprazole - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Omeprazole
Section: Adverse Reactions

Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 2%) in adults are headache, abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, and flatulence. In pediatric patients: respiratory system events, fever.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Omeprazole - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Omeprazole
Section: Drug Interactions

Clopidogrel: Concomitant use reduces exposure to the active metabolite of clopidogrel and decreases antiplatelet activity; avoid co-administration. Drugs dependent on gastric pH for absorption (ketoconazole, iron salts, erlotinib, mycophenolate mofetil): Omeprazole decreases absorption. Diazepam, Warfarin, Phenytoin: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19 and may prolong elimination. Methotrexate: Concomitant PPI use may elevate and prolong methotrexate levels; consider temporary PPI withdrawal.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Pantoprazole - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Pantoprazole
Section: Indications & Usage

Protonix is a proton pump inhibitor indicated for: Short-term treatment (up to 8 weeks) in the healing and symptomatic relief of erosive esophagitis associated with gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD); Maintenance of healing of erosive esophagitis; Long-term treatment of pathological hypersecretory conditions, including Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Pantoprazole - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Pantoprazole
Section: Dosage & Administration

Take with or without food. Swallow tablets whole; do not split, chew, or crush. Treatment of Erosive Esophagitis: 40 mg once daily for up to 8 weeks; an additional 8 weeks may be considered if unhealed. Maintenance of Healing: 40 mg once daily. Pathological Hypersecretion (Zollinger-Ellison): 40 mg twice daily, adjusted up to 240 mg daily.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Pantoprazole - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Pantoprazole
Section: Contraindications

Known hypersensitivity to pantoprazole or substituted benzimidazoles. Co-administration with rilpivirine-containing products.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Pantoprazole - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Pantoprazole
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Presence of gastric malignancy not ruled out by symptomatic response. Acute tubulointerstitial nephritis. Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD). Increased risk of osteoporosis-related fractures of hip, wrist, or spine with high-dose long-term use. Severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCAR / SJS / TEN). Cutaneous and systemic lupus erythematosus. Cyanocobalamin (Vitamin B12) deficiency with long-term therapy. Hypomagnesemia with long-term therapy.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Pantoprazole - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Pantoprazole
Section: Adverse Reactions

Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 2%) include headache, diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, flatulence, dizziness, and arthralgia.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Pantoprazole - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Pantoprazole
Section: Drug Interactions

Rilpivirine, atazanavir, nelfinavir: Concomitant use contraindicated due to loss of antiviral efficacy. Warfarin: Monitor INR/prothrombin time; increases in INR reported. Methotrexate: Elevated serum levels. Drugs dependent on gastric pH (ketoconazole, iron salts): Decreased absorption. Clopidogrel: Pantoprazole has less inhibitory effect on CYP2C19 than omeprazole.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Ondansetron - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Ondansetron
Section: Indications & Usage

Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist indicated for: Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with highly emetogenic cancer chemotherapy (HEC); Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with moderately emetogenic cancer chemotherapy (MEC); Prevention of nausea and vomiting associated with radiation therapy (total body irradiation, single high-dose fraction, or daily fractions); Prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV).

metadata.dosage_form: Tablet / Orally Disintegrating Tablet / Oral Solution / Injection

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Ondansetron - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Ondansetron
Section: Dosage & Administration

Highly Emetogenic Chemotherapy (HEC): Single 24 mg dose taken 30 minutes before start of single-day chemotherapy. Moderately Emetogenic Chemotherapy (MEC): 8 mg dose taken 30 minutes before chemotherapy, followed by 8 mg 8 hours after initial dose, then 8 mg twice daily for 1 to 2 days. Radiation Therapy: 8 mg 1 to 2 hours before radiation. PONV: 16 mg orally 1 hour before induction of anesthesia. In severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh score >= 10), total daily dose should not exceed 8 mg.

metadata.dosage_form: Tablet / Orally Disintegrating Tablet / Oral Solution / Injection

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Ondansetron - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Ondansetron
Section: Contraindications

Concomitant use of apomorphine (causes profound hypotension and loss of consciousness). Known hypersensitivity to ondansetron.

metadata.dosage_form: Tablet / Orally Disintegrating Tablet / Oral Solution / Injection

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Ondansetron - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Ondansetron
Section: Warnings & Precautions

QT Interval Prolongation and Torsades de Pointes: Dose-dependent QT prolongation; avoid in patients with congenital long QT syndrome. Serotonin Syndrome: Reported when used in combination with other serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, triptans). Myocardial Ischemia: Coronary artery vasospasm reported. Masking of Progressive Ileus and Gastric Distention after abdominal surgery.

title: Tramadol - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Tramadol
Section: Indications & Usage

Tramadol hydrochloride tablets are indicated in adults for the management of pain severe enough to require an opioid analgesic and for which alternative treatments are inadequate.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Tramadol - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Tramadol
Section: Dosage & Administration

Immediate-Release: 50 mg to 100 mg orally every 4 to 6 hours as needed for pain relief. Maximum daily dose is 400 mg per day. In patients over 75 years of age, maximum recommended dose is 300 mg/day in divided doses. Renal Impairment (CrCl < 30 mL/min): Increase dosing interval to every 12 hours (maximum 200 mg/day). Severe Hepatic Impairment (cirrhosis): 50 mg every 12 hours.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Tramadol - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Tramadol
Section: Contraindications

Children younger than 12 years of age. Postoperative management in children younger than 18 years following tonsillectomy or adenoidectomy. Significant respiratory depression. Acute or severe bronchial asthma. Known or suspected gastrointestinal obstruction, including paralytic ileus. Concomitant use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or use within the last 14 days.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Tramadol - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Tramadol
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Addiction, abuse, and misuse. Life-threatening respiratory depression. Ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolism leading to opioid toxicity in children and nursing infants. Neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome. Severe hypotension. Serotonin Syndrome: Potentially life-threatening when co-administered with serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans, TCAs). Seizure Risk: Can cause seizures; risk increased in patients taking medications that lower seizure threshold (antidepressants, neuroleptics) or with history of seizures. Suicide Risk. Adrenal Insufficiency.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Tramadol - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Tramadol
Section: Adverse Reactions

Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 5%) are dizziness, vertigo, nausea, constipation, headache, somnolence, vomiting, pruritus, CNS stimulation, asthenia, sweating, dyspepsia, and dry mouth.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Tramadol - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Tramadol
Section: Drug Interactions

Serotonergic Drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAOIs, triptans): High risk of serotonin syndrome. Benzodiazepines and CNS Depressants: Profound sedation and respiratory depression. CYP2D6 Inhibitors (quinidine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion): Increase tramadol concentrations and reduce active M1 metabolite. CYP3A4 Inhibitors (erythromycin, ketoconazole) / Inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine).

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Tramadol - Boxed Warning
content:
Drug: Tramadol
Section: Boxed Warning

WARNING: ADDICTION, ABUSE, AND MISUSE; RISK EVALUATION AND MITIGATION STRATEGY (REMS); LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION; ACCIDENTAL INGESTION; ULTRA-RAPID METABOLISM OF TRAMADOL AND OTHER RISK FACTORS FOR LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION IN CHILDREN; NEONATAL OPIOID WITHDRAWAL SYNDROME; INTERACTIONS WITH DRUGS AFFECTING CYTOCHROME P450 ISOENZYMES; AND RISKS FROM CONCOMITANT USE WITH BENZODIAZEPINES OR OTHER CNS DEPRESSANTS. Tramadol exposes patients and other users to the risks of opioid addiction, abuse, and misuse. Serious, life-threatening, or fatal respiratory depression may occur. Concomitant use with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants may result in profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death. Life-threatening respiratory depression and death have occurred in children who received tramadol who were ultra-rapid metabolizers of tramadol due to a CYP2D6 polymorphism.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Sertraline - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Sertraline
Section: Indications & Usage

Sertraline hydrochloride is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) indicated for the treatment of: Major depressive disorder (MDD); Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) in adults and pediatric patients aged 6 years and older; Panic disorder; Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD); Social anxiety disorder (SAD); Premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD).

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Sertraline - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Sertraline
Section: Dosage & Administration

Administer once daily, morning or evening. MDD and OCD: Starting dose is 50 mg once daily. Panic Disorder, PTSD, and SAD: Starting dose is 25 mg once daily, increased to 50 mg once daily after one week. Maximum dose is 200 mg once daily. PMDD: 50 mg/day either continuously or during luteal phase.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Sertraline - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Sertraline
Section: Contraindications

Concomitant use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or within 14 days of discontinuing an MAOI (causes fatal serotonin syndrome). Concomitant use of pimozide (increases pimozide levels and QT prolongation). Known hypersensitivity to sertraline.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Sertraline - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Sertraline
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Serotonin Syndrome: Potentially life-threatening when used with other serotonergic agents (triptans, tricyclic antidepressants, fentanyl, lithium, tramadol, buspirone, amphetamines, St. John's Wort). Increased Risk of Bleeding: Inhibit platelet serotonin reuptake; additive risk with NSAIDs, aspirin, or warfarin. Activation of Mania/Hypomania in bipolar disorder. Seizures. Angle-Closure Glaucoma. Hyponatremia / SIADH. Sexual Dysfunction. Discontinuation Syndrome upon abrupt cessation.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Sertraline - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Sertraline
Section: Adverse Reactions

Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 5% and twice placebo): nausea, diarrhea/loose stools, tremor, dyspepsia, decreased appetite, hyperhidrosis, ejaculation failure, and insomnia.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Sertraline - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Sertraline
Section: Drug Interactions

MAOIs: Contraindicated (serotonin syndrome). Pimozide: Contraindicated. Drugs affecting hemostasis (NSAIDs, aspirin, warfarin): Increase risk of bleeding. Serotonergic Drugs: Increase serotonin syndrome risk. CYP2D6 Substrates (propafenone, flecainide, TCAs): Sertraline can increase plasma levels.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Sertraline - Boxed Warning
content:
Drug: Sertraline
Section: Boxed Warning

WARNING: SUICIDAL THOUGHTS AND BEHAVIORS. Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for clinical worsening, and for emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Sertraline is not approved for use in pediatric patients except for patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD).

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Duloxetine - Indications & Usage
content:
Drug: Duloxetine
Section: Indications & Usage

Cymbalta is a serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) indicated for: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD); Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) in adults and pediatric patients aged 7 years and older; Diabetic Peripheral Neuropathic Pain (DPNP); Fibromyalgia; Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain (chronic lower back pain and chronic osteoarthritis pain).

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Duloxetine - Dosage & Administration
content:
Drug: Duloxetine
Section: Dosage & Administration

Administer orally with or without food. Swallow capsules whole; do not chew, crush, or open. MDD: 40 mg/day (20 mg twice daily) to 60 mg/day (once daily or 30 mg twice daily); maximum dose 120 mg/day. GAD: 60 mg once daily. DPNP: 60 mg once daily. Fibromyalgia: 60 mg once daily. Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain: 60 mg once daily. Discontinue gradually.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Duloxetine - Contraindications
content:
Drug: Duloxetine
Section: Contraindications

Concomitant use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) or within 14 days of stopping an MAOI (serotonin syndrome). Concomitant use with linezolid or methylene blue. Known hypersensitivity to duloxetine.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Duloxetine - Warnings & Precautions
content:
Drug: Duloxetine
Section: Warnings & Precautions

Hepatotoxicity: Hepatic failure, sometimes fatal, reported; avoid in patients with substantial alcohol use or chronic liver disease. Orthostatic Hypotension, Falls, and Syncope: Blood pressure and heart rate monitoring recommended. Serotonin Syndrome. Increased Risk of Bleeding with NSAIDs/aspirin/anticoagulants. Severe Skin Reactions (erythema multiforme, SJS). Discontinuation Syndrome upon abrupt cessation. Activation of Mania/Hypomania. Angle-Closure Glaucoma. Seizures. Blood Pressure Increases. Urinary Hesitation and Retention.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Duloxetine - Adverse Reactions
content:
Drug: Duloxetine
Section: Adverse Reactions

Most common adverse reactions (incidence >= 5% and at least twice placebo): nausea, dry mouth, somnolence, constipation, decreased appetite, hyperhidrosis, fatigue, and dizziness.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Duloxetine - Drug Interactions
content:
Drug: Duloxetine
Section: Drug Interactions

MAOIs: Contraindicated. Potent CYP1A2 Inhibitors (fluvoxamine, ciprofloxacin): Concomitant use should be avoided as it produces marked increases in duloxetine exposure. CYP2D6 Inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine, quinidine): Increase duloxetine levels. Serotonergic Drugs: Risk of serotonin syndrome. Drugs affecting hemostasis (NSAIDs, warfarin): Increased bleeding risk.

publisher: U.S. National Library of Medicine / FDA
title: Duloxetine - Boxed Warning
content:
Drug: Duloxetine
Section: Boxed Warning

WARNING: SUICIDAL THOUGHTS AND BEHAVIORS. Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for clinical worsening, and for emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Duloxetine is not approved for use in pediatric patients.
